candidates.attacker_control: The content of any file in the build workspace matching the job's `testResults` pattern (e.g. `**/TEST-*.xml` via the JUnit post-build publisher or `junit testResults: '...'` pipeline step). Workspace files are written by the build itself (test framework, build script, checked-out SCM content, untrusted PR builds), so an attacker who can influence build/test output or run code in the build can write a report file containing `<!DOCTYPE ... [ <!ENTITY ... SYSTEM "file:///...|http://..."> ]>`. The pattern itself is taken from job config and expanded from the build environment (JUnitResultArchiver.java:164), while the malicious payload is in the file content. Only the file modification-time filter (TestResult.java:202-209) applies, which a build-time-written report satisfies.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched all main sources for hardening: no `disallow-doctype`, `setFeature`, `external-general-entities`, `XMLReader`, `SAXParser`, DocumentBuilder/TransformerFactory usage anywhere (only one XML parser exists: SuiteResult's SAXReader), so there is no mitigation elsewere in the plugin. Verified the installed resolver does not block: XMLEntityResolver.java:55-70 redirects only `http://testng.org/*` to classpath resources and returns `null` in the default fallback, which delegates to standard resolution rather than refusing it. Verified upstream of the parse there is only a pattern/time filter (JUnitResultArchiver.java:159-166; TestResult.java:198-227) and no content validation or DOCTYPE rejection. Verified the parse runs on the node holding the workspace (JUnitParser.java:114, MasterToSlaveFileCallable), not behind any output-escaping UI layer. Noted that the tree already contains unused XXE payload fixtures `src/test/resources/hudson/tasks/junit/testXxe-xxe.xml` (DOCTYPE + `SYSTEM "$OOB_LINK$"` parameter entity) and `testXxe-oob.xml`, confirming this report format carries such payloads and that the corresponding negative test is absent from the snapshot.
candidates.impact: XML External Entity injection against the Jenkins controller/agent that parses the report: (1) disclosure of local files readable by the Jenkins process (credentials files, configuration, agent secrets) with blind/OOB exfiltration via parameter entities chained from an attacker DTD; (2) SSRF - the parser fetches arbitrary http(s)/file URLs from that host, reachable to internal services; (3) denial of service via entity expansion ("billion laughs"/recursive parameter entities) during build result parsing. Because untrusted build content triggers the parse (a normal CI threat model in Jenkins, especially with untrusted PR builds or shared agents), a single crafted test report compromises the parsing machine.
candidates.prerequisites: A job using the JUnit plugin (freestyle `JUnitResultArchiver` or pipeline `junit` step) whose glob matches an attacker-writable report file; parsing executes on the machine that owns the workspace (`workspace.act(new ParseResultCallable(...))`, JUnitParser.java:114) - a Jenkins agent, or the Jenkins controller when the build/workspace is on the controller. The JDK/JAXP (Xerces) and dom4j version bundled by Jenkins core must keep the default permissive handling of DOCTYPE/external entities (no hardening exists in this snapshot; the resolver deliberately falls back to default resolution).
candidates.root_cause: SuiteResult.parse creates `new SAXReader()` and only calls `setEntityResolver(new XMLEntityResolver())`; it never disables DOCTYPE processing or external entity resolution (no `http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl`, `external-general-entities`, `external-parameter-entities`, or ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/SCHEMA restrictions). The resolver that is installed provides no restriction either: `XMLEntityResolver.resolveEntity` returns `null` for every systemId that does not start with `http://testng.org/` (only TestNG system-ids are remapped to classpath resources), and `null` means "let the underlying SAX/JAXP parser resolve it by default", i.e. dereference the URI (file:/// or http://). Consequently any DOCTYPE/entity declaration in a JUnit report file is honoured by the parser with default, permissive settings.
candidates.title: XXE: JUnit report XML parsed with unrestricted dom4j SAXReader (SuiteResult.parse)
candidates.trace: junit step/JUnitResultArchiver.perform -> JUnitResultArchiver.parseAndAttach (line 153/159, pattern expanded at 164) -> JUnitParser.parseResult (104-116) -> `workspace.act(new ParseResultCallable(...))` -> ParseResultCallable.invoke on the agent (137-147) builds an Ant FileSet/DirectoryScanner and constructs TestResult -> TestResult.parse (198-227) -> parsePossiblyEmpty (274-283) -> parse(File, PipelineTestDetails) (346-348) -> SuiteResult.parse (159-169): `SAXReader saxReader = new SAXReader(); saxReader.setEntityResolver(new XMLEntityResolver()); ... saxReader.read(xmlReportStream)` -> for a systemId not starting with http://testng.org/, XMLEntityResolver.resolveEntity returns null (line 69-70) -> the underlying parser performs default resolution of the external entity (local file or URL), and parameter entities declared in the DOCTYPE can be chained for out-of-band exfiltration. Parse failures are caught in TestResult.parse (352-366) and turned into a `[failed-to-read]` CaseResult containing the exception stack trace, which is surfaced in the build's test report.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and not exploit-tested (no code execution permitted). The dom4j version actually resolved from Jenkins core is not visible in this snapshot; the finding assumes it (and the JDK's JAXP/Xerces) keeps DOCTYPE and external-entity resolution enabled by default - true for dom4j of this era and for the historical Jenkins JUnit plugin issue, but not verifiable from the assigned files. Exact exfiltration shape (reflected vs. blind) depends on how the resolved content is embedded in the report XML; OOB and DoS impact does not depend on reflection. Reachability requires a job configuration whose pattern matches an attacker-written file, which depends on deployment configuration, not on this source tree.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (XXE)

coverage_summary: Scope: 448 source-root files, 447 model-visible (1 file excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter); 60 Java files (34 main, 26 test) plus properties/html/xml resources. I read all main Java sources relevant to test-result ingestion and rendering data sources: `hudson/tasks/junit/{SuiteResult, TestResult, CaseResult, JUnitParser, JUnitResultArchiver, JUnitResultsStep, JUnitResultsStepExecution, XMLEntityResolver, TestResultAction, History, TestObject, TimeToFloat, TestNameTransformer, TestDataPublisher}` and the shared `hudson/tasks/test/{TestObject, AbstractTestResultAction, AggregatedTestResultPublisher, DefaultTestResultParserImpl, TestResultParser}`; plus test resources/hints. P1 relation index: 60/60 Java files parsed, 0 parse errors, 1020 symbols, 3024 call sites, 2219 unresolved calls, no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution; the index's `SuiteResult`/`security_call` facts were used only to navigate and every edge in the submitted trace was confirmed by reading the source text. Unreviewed/not available: Jelly view templates (none present in the snapshot), Jenkins core classes (dom4j, XStream2, FilePath, Digester) that live in dependencies outside this tree, non-English i18n property files beyond spot checks, and the one excluded sensitive file.
limitations: Not runtime-confirmed: no code, tests, or parsers were executed; exploitability of the XXE depends on the dom4j/JAXP versions resolved from Jenkins core, which are not part of the assigned snapshot.

No dependency tree or resolved-jar inspection was possible, so the parser's default DOCTYPE/entity behaviour is inferred from the absence of any hardening calls plus historical behaviour, not observed.
The view layer (jelly templates) is absent from the snapshot, so UI-level issues (XSS/escaping) could not be assessed at all.
The P1 index reports no control-flow/data-flow and 2219 unresolved calls; call-path claims were therefore verified manually in source, and the index cannot prove reachability.
1 source file is hidden by the sensitive-name/path filter and was not reviewed.

rejected_leads.lead: Stored/reflected XSS from attacker-controlled test names, stdout/stderr, failure messages or descriptions rendered into test-report pages.
rejected_leads.reason: The Java sources only return raw strings (e.g. CaseResult.getStdout, SuiteResult.getName, TestObject.getDescription); no HTML construction exists in the snapshot and all `*.jelly` view templates are absent from the assigned files, so no unescaped output binding can be evidenced. Unverifiable from this snapshot, not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: Directory traversal via the Surefire companion-file read: `new File(xmlReport.getParentFile(), m.group(1) + "-output.txt")` (SuiteResult.java:259-271).
rejected_leads.reason: `m.group(1)` comes from `xmlReport.getName()` matched against `TEST-(.+)\.xml`, so it is the final path component and cannot contain a separator; the read is confined to the report's own directory and requires the file to exist. No traversal or arbitrary-read evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing authorization check on test-result description submission (`doSubmitDescription`).
rejected_leads.reason: `hudson.tasks.test.TestObject.doSubmitDescription` (lines 453-465) calls `getRun().checkPermission(Run.UPDATE)` before `setDescription(...)`/`save()`. The check is present, so no finding.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsafe deserialization of the persisted `junitResult.xml` via XStream (TestResultAction.java:302-309 / 131-133).
rejected_leads.reason: Uses Jenkins' hardened `XStream2` with only three type aliases and a `HeapSpaceStringConverter`; the file lives inside the run directory and this snapshot shows no path by which an unprivileged attacker writes it. No source-level attacker control demonstrated - rejected as a weaker, speculative lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Classpath resource lookup driven by attacker-supplied systemId in `XMLEntityResolver` (`http://testng.org/<name>` -> `ClassLoader.getResource(name)`).
rejected_leads.reason: Reads classpath resources only (not arbitrary filesystem paths) and is entirely overshadowed by the XXE candidate in the same class; no concrete disclosure path shown.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in the `testResults` glob (Ant FileSet / DirectoryScanner / FilePath.list).
rejected_leads.reason: Uses Ant pattern matching rooted at the workspace (`Util.createFileSet(ws, testResults)`), and the UI validation path uses `FilePath.validateFileMask`; no evidence that absolute paths or `..` escape the workspace, and the file content issue is the more impactful one.

summary: The snapshot is the Jenkins JUnit plugin (pom artifactId `junit`, version `1.24-SNAPSHOT`, Jenkins core 2.7.3). I traced the JUnit XML report parsing path from the `junit` pipeline step / `JUnitResultArchiver` post-build step down to `SuiteResult.parse`, which builds a dom4j `SAXReader` without disabling DOCTYPE/external entities and with an `XMLEntityResolver` whose fallback returns `null` (default resolution). This leaves the parser resolving attacker-supplied external entities in report files that a build can place in the workspace, i.e. a classic XXE / CWE-611. This is the single strongest candidate; other leads (XSS in views, output-file companion read, permission checks, XStream deserialization, classpath lookup) were examined and rejected or marked unverifiable. No code was executed; all claims are source-text level.
